title: Bill Bruford - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 162,805 (the rest navigation boxes). William Scott Bruford, born 17 May 1949, Sevenoaks, Kent; New Beacon School, then Tonbridge School. Took up the drums at 13 after watching American jazz drummers on BBC2's Jazz 625; names Max Roach, Joe Morello, Art Blakey and Ginger Baker as his most influential drummers; a Jim Chapin tutor from a schoolfriend, a few lessons from Lou Pocock of the Royal Philharmonic; practised with brushes on album sleeves, 'a perfect education'. The Breed (1966-67); Yes from June 1968 to 19 July 1972 (Yes, Time and a Word, The Yes Album, Fragile, Close to the Edge); King Crimson 1972-74, 1981-84, 1994-97 (Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Starless and Bible Black, Red, Discipline, Beat, Three of a Perfect Pair, Vrooom, Thrak), 'where you could play in 17/16 and still stay in decent hotels'; Gong (late 1974); National Health (1975-77); Genesis's concert drummer on the A Trick of the Tail tour (March-July 1976); his band Bruford (Feels Good to Me 1978, One of a Kind 1979, Gradually Going Tornado 1980); U.K. (1978) with John Wetton and Allan Holdsworth; Moraz/Bruford (1983-85); Earthworks (1986-93, 1997-2008); Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe (1988-90) and Union (1991), 'the worst record I've ever been on'. Early on he developed unusual beat placement and time signatures, partly because Chris Squire played high in the bass's register. Simmons electronic drums with an acoustic kit on King Crimson's 1981-84 records and later with Earthworks; dropped in 1997. Retired 1 January 2009 after 2,885 gigs, the last with Earthworks at Ronnie Scott's on 31 July 2008. PhD in music, University of Surrey, 2016 ('Making it work: Creative music performance and the Western kit drummer'). Modern Drummer Hall of Fame 1990; Rolling Stone No. 16 of 100 (2016); Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Yes (2017). Matt Cameron: 'Listening to a lot of Bruford prepared me supremely to play in Soundgarden', and his 'placement of fives and sevens'.

title: Bill Bruford, 'Equipment' (billbruford.com)
notes: His own inventory by year. 1968-69 Premier Olympic; 1969-71 Ludwig, a 14x5 Ludwig Supraphonic LM400; 1971-72 Hayman in 'natural pine', a Supraphonic or a 14x5.5 wood Hayman snare, Paiste (15 Giant Beat hats, 602 crashes and ride), a cowbell; 1972-73 Ludwig and Hayman, a 14x6.5 Ludwig Supersensitive, a Premier timbale, Paiste 2002, tuned gongs, woodblock, cowbell, metal plates; 1974-80 Hayman and Ludwig in natural wood with the Supersensitive, Paiste 2002 and 602, Remo Roto Toms from 1977, a 20-inch China; 1981-82 Tama Superstar (light blue), a Simmons SDS5 (six pads on the kit, five on the front frame, an electronic bass drum), a 14-inch Roto Tom, a 22-inch Tama gong drum, five 6-inch Dragon drums, a slit drum; 1982-83 Tama Superstar in natural birch, four low Octobans; 1983-84 a Simmons SDS7; 1985-86 SDS9; 1987-98 Simmons SDX; Tama Starclassic later. Snare 'usually tuned tight, with the bottom slightly tighter than the top'; toms medium tight, both heads at about the same pitch.

title: John Natelli, '10 Ways To Sound Like Bill Bruford', DRUM!, 22 November 2012
notes: Read as text; its notated examples are images, not read. The Fragile snare 'a sort of dry, punchy bonk'; a sixteenth on the bass drum just before the backbeat; ghosted breakbeat patterns in Yours Is No Disgrace and Siberian Khatru; Roundabout a similar feel differently built. The snare: Ludwig Supra-Phonics and Supersensitives, rimshots about halfway between the center and the rim, the head 'fairly tight'; 'I just let my drums ring, and those harmonics are part of the music.' Paradiddle variations for 7/4 phrases; Beelzebub (9/8) on Feels Good to Me (1978); the paradiddle-diddle in Heart of the Sunrise and Easy Money. Single-stroke sextuplets as fill material. Discipline (1981): a phrase of 17 sixteenths against quarter notes on the bass drum, so the foot does not meet the downbeat again for four measures; In the Dead of Night. Polyrhythms implied by orchestration around the kit: on Red, in One More Red Nightmare and the title track, a 3:2 outlined round the toms and ride (Ex. 5), after Tony Williams and Elvin Jones. Backbeat displaced in Sample and Hold (New York radio, 1979); in Siberian Khatru the backbeat kept while the band moves through odd-metered phrases. The symmetrical kit of the late 1990s. Soloing over Indiscipline's vamp (Mohawk College clinic, 2006), returning to the downbeat only occasionally.

title: Scott K. Fish, 'Bill Bruford', Modern Drummer, July 1983 (transcript at Elephant Talk)
notes: The King Crimson kit: 'a hybrid kit of half electric/half acoustic', 'an "internal" acoustic kit which is fairly conventional': Tama bass drum and snare, a 14-inch Roto-Tom and a big Tama gong tom, Octobans ('They're Dragon Drums actually'); 'about 11 Simmons pads now in the show'; the Simmons 'is pitchable and it has a peculiar melodic sound', 'It's dictating some of the way King Crimson is going'; 'The sticks that used to be between two sound sources of cymbal and snare, perhaps are now between four sound sources.' The Waiting Man (Beat) is played 'because I had the Simmons drums up to certain pitches'; Discipline 'the flag tune of that idea'. 'It's even remotely possible to play anything in 17/16 and stay in a decent hotel'; 'perhaps in a multiple meter over the dance groove in the feet'; 'One is always trying to present the simple and the complex at the same time.' Jazz first: 'I had stacks of Blue Note records', 'I borrowed somebody else's roots'. Of Jack DeJohnette: 'I do hear melody in his drumming.'

title: Saku Mantere, 'A Conversation With Bill Bruford. Part One: Drumming', Pienemmät Purot, 11 May 2019
notes: 'I always had considerable interest in time signatures and meters, much less in metronomic tempo.' 'How I address time is a mystery to me too ... I sit. I play.' Groove 'something I create and share with others'. 'The parts on the early Yes albums were tightly organized'; playing Close to the Edge differently every night 'eventually caused irritation'. Listeners recognise his snare, he says, not 'so much [from] the sound of the snare drum as its typically unusual placement in the measure'. His King Crimson roles: 'the terrorist-renegade (Indiscipline)', 'the colourist (Sheltering Sky)'. 'Timbral and dynamic variations were playgrounds of delight, especially with the onset of electronics.' 'The complex becomes simple when you can do it: the art is to conceal the art.' Morello and Brubeck as the frame for his rhythmic ideas.

title: Eoghan Lyng, 'King Crimson's Bill Bruford names his favourite drummers', Far Out, 28 April 2022
notes: From an interview with Far Out: 'all the great jazz drummers of the day, such as Max Roach'; 'Joe Morello from Dave Brubeck Quartet'; 'perhaps Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. Fantastic group, big sound', and 'if you were in Art Blakey's group in 1965, the music didn't go anywhere until the drummer said so.'

title: Fragile (Yes album) - Wikipedia
notes: Released 12 November 1971 (UK), 4 January 1972 (US), Atlantic. Recorded at Advision, London, August-September 1971; produced by Yes and Eddy Offord. Bruford: drums, percussion; he wrote Five per Cent for Nothing, 'his first attempt at composition', and co-wrote Heart of the Sunrise; he suggested the album's title. Roundabout (Anderson, Howe), Long Distance Runaround (Anderson).

title: Close to the Edge - Wikipedia
notes: Released 8 September 1972 (UK), Atlantic; recorded April-June 1972 at Advision; produced by Yes and Eddy Offord. Siberian Khatru (Anderson, Howe, Wakeman). Bruford found the democratic writing 'unbelievably hard work', wanted more jazz and improvisation, and left on 19 July 1972 for King Crimson; Alan White learned the parts in about three days for the tour from 30 July.

title: Larks' Tongues in Aspic - Wikipedia
notes: Released 23 March 1973, Island (UK), Atlantic (US); recorded January-February 1973 at Command Studios, London; produced by King Crimson. Bruford: drums; Jamie Muir: percussion, drums, 'allsorts'. Part Two (instrumental) by Fripp.

title: Red (King Crimson album) - Wikipedia
notes: Released 7 October 1974, Island; recorded July-August 1974 at Olympic Studios, Barnes; produced by King Crimson. Bruford: drums, percussion, production. Red (instrumental, Fripp); One More Red Nightmare (Fripp, Wetton). Fripp called the Wetton-Bruford rhythm section 'a flying brick wall'. Bruford said he did not 'get' Red but trusted Fripp. Fripp disbanded the group on 24 September 1974.

title: Discipline (King Crimson album) - Wikipedia
notes: Released 2 October 1981, E.G. (UK), Warner Bros. (US); recorded May-June 1981 at Island Studios, London; produced by King Crimson and Rhett Davies. Bruford: 'drums, Simmons electronic drums, slit drum, percussion'. With Adrian Belew, Robert Fripp, Tony Levin.

title: U.K. (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Read through a search summary. Recorded December 1977 to January 1978 at Trident Studios, London; released April 1978 on E.G. and Polydor; produced by U.K. John Wetton, Eddie Jobson, Bill Bruford, Allan Holdsworth. The first three tracks form the In the Dead of Night suite; In the Dead of Night was edited for a single.
